CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Flashcards: 434 cards

434 free CompTIA Network+ flashcards from the course's cheat sheet and glossary. Tap a card to flip it. Mark the ones you know and they drop out of the deck; the rest keep coming back.

Space flips, arrow keys move. Known cards are remembered in this browser.

Acronyms 316

1000BASE-LX
Gigabit Ethernet, long wavelength. 1 Gbps over single-mode fiber to 10 km (also works on multimode for short runs).
1000BASE-SX
Gigabit Ethernet, short wavelength. 1 Gbps over multimode fiber to about 550 m.
1000BASE-T
Gigabit Ethernet over twisted pair. 1 Gbps over Cat 5e or better to 100 m, using all four pairs.
100BASE-TX
Fast Ethernet over twisted pair. 100 Mbps over Cat 5 or better using two pairs.
10BASE-T
Ethernet over twisted pair. The original 10 Mbps twisted-pair Ethernet.
10GBASE-ER
10 Gigabit Ethernet, extended reach. 10 Gbps over single-mode fiber to 40 km.
10GBASE-LR
10 Gigabit Ethernet, long reach. 10 Gbps over single-mode fiber to 10 km.
10GBASE-SR
10 Gigabit Ethernet, short reach. 10 Gbps over multimode fiber, about 300 m on OM3, 400 m on OM4.
10GBASE-T
10 Gigabit Ethernet over twisted pair. 10 Gbps over Cat 6A to 100 m (Cat 6 to 55 m).
40GBASE-T
40 Gigabit Ethernet over twisted pair. 40 Gbps over Cat 8 to 30 m.
4G
Fourth-generation cellular. The LTE generation of mobile broadband.
5G
Fifth-generation cellular. The current mobile network generation with higher speed and lower latency than LTE.
802.11
IEEE 802.11. The family of Wi-Fi standards.
802.1AX
IEEE 802.1AX. The current standard for link aggregation, using LACP.
802.1D
IEEE 802.1D. The original spanning tree standard.
802.1Q
IEEE 802.1Q. The VLAN tagging standard: a 4-byte tag in the Ethernet frame carries the VLAN ID on trunks.
802.1s
IEEE 802.1s. Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol.
802.1w
IEEE 802.1w. Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol.
802.1X
IEEE 802.1X. Port-based network access control: a device must authenticate before the switch port or Wi-Fi passes traffic.
802.3ad
IEEE 802.3ad. The original link aggregation standard, now part of 802.1AX.
802.3af
IEEE 802.3af. The original Power over Ethernet standard: about 15.4 W at the switch, 12.95 W at the device.
802.3at
IEEE 802.3at. PoE+: about 30 W at the switch, 25.5 W at the device.
802.3bt
IEEE 802.3bt. PoE++: 60 W (Type 3) or up to 90 W (Type 4) using all four pairs.
8P8C
Eight position, eight contact. The formal name of the connector everyone calls RJ45.
AAA
Authentication, authorization, and accounting. Prove who you are, decide what you may do, record what you did.
AAAA
Quad-A record. The DNS record that maps a name to an IPv6 address.
ACK
Acknowledgment. The TCP flag or message confirming data arrived.
ACL
Access control list. An ordered list of permit and deny rules on a router, firewall, or file system.
AD
Administrative distance. A router's trust ranking for route sources; the lowest wins when two protocols offer the same prefix.
AES
Advanced Encryption Standard. The standard symmetric cipher, with 128, 192, or 256-bit keys.
AH
Authentication Header. The IPsec protocol that provides integrity and authentication without encryption.
AP
Access point. The radio that bridges Wi-Fi clients onto the wired network.
APC
Angled physical contact. A fiber connector polish with an 8-degree angle (green) that reflects less light.
API
Application programming interface. The defined way one program talks to another, such as the web endpoints a cloud service exposes.
APIPA
Automatic Private IP Addressing. The 169.254.x.x address a host gives itself when it cannot reach a DHCP server.
ARP
Address Resolution Protocol. Finds the MAC address that goes with a known IPv4 address on the local segment.
AS
Autonomous system. A network under one administration with its own routing policy, identified by a number for BGP.
ASCII
American Standard Code for Information Interchange. The character encoding that maps letters and symbols to numbers 0 to 127.
AUP
Acceptable use policy. The rules for how staff may use company systems and data.
BASE
Baseband. The middle of Ethernet names: the cable carries one digital signal at a time.
BGP
Border Gateway Protocol. The path-vector routing protocol of the internet, between autonomous systems.
BNC
Bayonet Neill-Concelman connector. The twist-lock coax connector used on older LANs, test equipment, and CCTV.
BPDU
Bridge protocol data unit. The frames switches exchange to build the spanning tree.
BSSID
Basic service set identifier. The MAC address of one access point radio, which identifies that specific cell.
BYOD
Bring your own device. Staff use personal phones and laptops for work.
CA
Certificate authority. The trusted entity that signs certificates.
CAM
Content-addressable memory (table). The switch's MAC address table.
CAN
Campus area network. A network spanning several buildings on one campus.
CASB
Cloud access security broker. Sits between users and cloud apps to enforce policy, visibility, and data protection.
CCMP
Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol. The AES-based encryption WPA2 uses.
CDN
Content delivery network. Caches content on servers around the world so users fetch it from nearby.
CDP
Cisco Discovery Protocol. Cisco's Layer 2 protocol for learning what device is on the other end of a link.
CIA
Confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The three goals of security: keep data secret, keep it correct, keep it reachable.
CIDR
Classless inter-domain routing. Prefix notation for subnets, such as /24, replacing the old A, B, C classes.
CNAME
Canonical name record. A DNS alias: one name points to another name.
CPU
Central processing unit. The processor that executes instructions.
CRC
Cyclic redundancy check. The checksum in an Ethernet frame trailer; CRC errors mean the frame was damaged in transit.
CRM
Customer relationship management. Software for tracking customers and sales, usually SaaS.
CSMA/CD
Carrier sense multiple access with collision detection. The original Ethernet rule: listen before sending, and back off if a collision is heard.
DaaS
Desktop as a service. VDI hosted by a cloud provider.
DAC
Direct attach cable. A twinaxial copper cable with transceivers permanently attached at both ends, for short 10 to 100 Gbps links.
DDoS
Distributed denial of service. Many sources, usually a botnet, flood a target at once.
DFS
Dynamic frequency selection. Wi-Fi channels in the 5 GHz band that must yield to radar.
DHCP
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. Hands out IP addresses, masks, gateways, and DNS servers automatically (UDP 67 and 68).
DKIM
DomainKeys Identified Mail. Outgoing mail is digitally signed; the public key is published in DNS.
DMARC
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance. A DNS policy telling receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF or DKIM, and where to send reports.
DMZ
Demilitarized zone. A screened subnet between the internet and the internal network for public-facing servers.
DNS
Domain Name System. Translates names such as www.example.com into IP addresses (UDP 53, TCP 53 for zone transfers).
DNS64
DNS 6 to 4. Synthesizes AAAA records for IPv4-only names so IPv6-only clients can reach them through NAT64.
DNSSEC
DNS Security Extensions. Digital signatures on DNS records so a resolver can tell an answer was not forged.
DoH
DNS over HTTPS. DNS queries carried inside HTTPS on TCP 443 so they cannot be read or altered in transit.
DORA
Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. The four-step DHCP lease exchange.
DoS
Denial of service. One source floods or crashes a target so it cannot serve users.
DoT
DNS over TLS. DNS queries encrypted with TLS on TCP 853.
DR
Disaster recovery. The plans and sites for restoring IT after a major outage.
DSS
Data Security Standard. The PCI DSS rules for protecting payment card data.
EGP
Exterior gateway protocol. A routing protocol between organizations; today that means BGP.
EIGRP
Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol. Cisco's advanced distance-vector protocol with fast convergence and a composite metric.
EMI
Electromagnetic interference. Noise from motors, power lines, fluorescent lights, and radios that corrupts signals on copper cable.
EOL
End of life. The vendor stops selling the product.
EOS
End of support. The vendor stops providing patches and help.
ER
Extended reach. The single-mode 10 Gbps optic for 40 km.
ESP
Encapsulating Security Payload. The IPsec protocol that encrypts and authenticates the payload.
ESSID
Extended service set identifier. The SSID shared by several access points so clients can roam between them.
EU
European Union. The political union whose GDPR privacy law reaches any company holding its residents' data.
EUI-64
Extended unique identifier, 64-bit. A way to build an IPv6 interface ID from a 48-bit MAC address.
FCC
Federal Communications Commission. The US regulator of radio spectrum, including Wi-Fi bands and transmit power.
FHRP
First-hop redundancy protocol. Lets two routers share one virtual gateway address so hosts keep working if one fails.
FIN
Finish flag. The TCP flag that closes a connection gracefully.
FTP
File Transfer Protocol. Plaintext file transfer on TCP 21 (control) and 20 (data); replace with SFTP or FTPS.
FTPS
FTP Secure. FTP wrapped in TLS, ports 990 and 989 (implicit) or 21 with an upgrade (explicit).
GBIC
Gigabit interface converter. The older, larger hot-swappable transceiver replaced by the SFP.
Gbps
Gigabits per second. Billions of bits per second; gigabit Ethernet is 1 Gbps.
GDPR
General Data Protection Regulation. The European Union's privacy law for personal data of EU residents.
GG45
GG45 connector. A backward-compatible Cat 7 and Cat 8 connector that also accepts RJ45 plugs.
GHz
Gigahertz. Billions of cycles per second; CPU clock speed and Wi-Fi band frequency.
GLBP
Gateway Load Balancing Protocol. Cisco's first-hop redundancy that also spreads traffic across several gateways.
GPS
Global Positioning System. Satellite positioning, also used as a stratum 0 time reference.
GRE
Generic Routing Encapsulation. A simple tunnel that wraps one packet inside another, with no encryption.
GUI
Graphical user interface. Windows, icons, and a mouse, as opposed to a command line.
HIPAA
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. The US law protecting health information and setting privacy and security rules.
HSRP
Hot Standby Router Protocol. Cisco's first-hop redundancy protocol: one active router, one standby, one virtual IP.
HTTP
Hypertext Transfer Protocol. Web traffic in the clear on TCP 80.
HTTPS
Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure. HTTP inside TLS on TCP 443.
IaaS
Infrastructure as a service. The provider supplies virtual machines, storage, and networks; you manage the operating system and up.
IaC
Infrastructure as code. Defining networks and servers in files that tools build automatically and repeatably.
IBSS
Independent basic service set. An ad hoc Wi-Fi network between devices with no access point.
ICMP
Internet Control Message Protocol. The messaging protocol behind ping and traceroute, and behind unreachable and time-exceeded errors.
ICS
Industrial control system. The general term for computers that run physical processes; SCADA is one kind.
ID
Identifier or identification. A name or number that uniquely labels a user, device, session, or record.
IDF
Intermediate distribution frame. A smaller wiring closet on a floor or wing that feeds back to the MDF.
IDS
Intrusion detection system. Watches a copy of the traffic and alerts on attacks; cannot block them.
IEEE
Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. The engineering body behind Ethernet (802.3), Wi-Fi (802.11), and many device standards.
IGMP
Internet Group Management Protocol. How hosts join and leave IPv4 multicast groups.
IGP
Interior gateway protocol. A routing protocol used inside one organization: OSPF, EIGRP, RIP, IS-IS.
IIoT
Industrial Internet of Things. Networked sensors and controllers in factories and utilities.
IKE
Internet Key Exchange. Negotiates the keys and security associations for IPsec; UDP 500, and 4500 through NAT.
IMAP
Internet Message Access Protocol. Reads mail that stays on the server, synced across devices; TCP 143, secure 993.
IMAPS
IMAP Secure. IMAP over TLS on TCP 993.
IoT
Internet of Things. Networked devices such as cameras, sensors, thermostats, and smart TVs.
IP
Internet Protocol. The Layer 3 protocol that addresses and routes packets between networks.
IPAM
IP address management. Software that tracks which addresses and subnets are in use.
IPFIX
IP Flow Information Export. The standard flow-export protocol, the successor of NetFlow.
IPS
Intrusion prevention system. Sits inline and blocks attacks as they pass.
IPsec
Internet Protocol Security. The suite that encrypts and authenticates IP packets for VPNs.
IPv4
Internet Protocol version 4. 32-bit addresses written as four decimal octets, such as 192.168.1.10.
IPv6
Internet Protocol version 6. 128-bit addresses in eight hex groups; no broadcast, built-in autoconfiguration.
IS-IS
Intermediate System to Intermediate System. A link-state interior routing protocol used mainly by large providers.
ISATAP
Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol. A tunneling method that carries IPv6 inside IPv4 within one organization.
iSCSI
Internet SCSI. SCSI storage commands over a TCP/IP network, giving block-level storage without Fibre Channel.
ISP
Internet service provider. The company that connects you to the internet.
IT
Information technology. Computers, networks, and the people who run them.
JPEG
Joint Photographic Experts Group (image format). The common compressed photo format.
LACP
Link Aggregation Control Protocol. Negotiates bundling several physical links into one logical link (802.1AX, formerly 802.3ad).
LAN
Local area network. One site's network: a building, floor, or campus that one organization owns and runs.
LC
Lucent connector. The small square snap-in fiber connector, the most common on modern transceivers.
LDAP
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. Queries a directory such as Active Directory for users and groups; TCP 389, secure 636.
LDAPS
LDAP Secure. LDAP over TLS on TCP 636.
LED
Light-emitting diode. A small light source: the status lights on a port, the lamp in cheap fiber transmitters, and modern display backlights.
LLC
Logical link control. The upper sublayer of the data link layer that identifies which network protocol a frame carries.
LLDP
Link Layer Discovery Protocol. The vendor-neutral neighbor discovery protocol (IEEE 802.1AB).
LR
Long reach. The single-mode 10 Gbps optic, 10 km.
LTE
Long-Term Evolution. 4G cellular data; the workhorse mobile broadband standard.
MAC
Media access control (address). The 48-bit hardware address burned into a network interface, used at Layer 2.
macOS
Mac operating system. Apple's desktop operating system.
MAN
Metropolitan area network. A city-sized network: bigger than a LAN, smaller than a WAN.
Mbps
Megabits per second. Millions of bits per second; the unit for network link speed.
MDF
Main distribution frame. The building's main wiring closet where outside lines and the core equipment land.
MDIX
Medium-dependent interface crossover. Auto-MDIX ports sense the cable and swap transmit and receive pairs, so crossover cables are rarely needed.
MFA
Multi-factor authentication. Two or more different kinds of proof: something you know, have, are, or where you are.
MHz
Megahertz. Millions of cycles per second; memory speed, radio channels, and older CPU clocks.
MIB
Management information base. The database of variables an SNMP agent exposes.
MIMO
Multiple input, multiple output. Using several antennas at once to send parallel data streams for more speed.
MMF
Multimode fiber. A wider core (50 or 62.5 microns) carrying many light paths, for hundreds of meters.
MOU
Memorandum of understanding. A non-binding statement of intent and roles between parties.
MPEG
Moving Picture Experts Group (video format). The family of compressed video formats.
MPLS
Multiprotocol Label Switching. A provider WAN that forwards by short labels instead of IP lookups, with traffic engineering and QoS.
MPO
Multi-fiber push-on connector. A ribbon connector carrying 12 or 24 fibers, used for 40 and 100 Gbps parallel optics.
ms
Millisecond. One thousandth of a second; latency and response times.
MSTP
Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol. Runs one spanning tree instance for a group of VLANs instead of one per VLAN.
MTBF
Mean time between failures. The average running time before a component fails; a reliability measure.
MTP
Multi-fiber termination push-on connector. A brand-name, higher-precision version of the MPO connector.
MTTR
Mean time to repair. The average time to fix a failure and restore service.
MTU
Maximum transmission unit. The largest packet a link can carry, 1500 bytes on standard Ethernet.
MU-MIMO
Multi-user MIMO. The access point serves several clients at the same time with separate streams.
MX
Mail exchanger record. The DNS record that says which server accepts email for a domain.
NAC
Network access control. Checks a device's identity and health before letting it onto the network.
NACL
Network access control list. A stateless rule set applied to a cloud subnet.
NAS
Network-attached storage. A file server appliance that shares folders over the regular network using SMB or NFS.
NAT
Network address translation. Rewrites private inside addresses to a public address at the router so many hosts can share it.
NAT-T
NAT traversal. Wraps IPsec in UDP 4500 so it can pass through address translation.
NAT64
Network address translation 6 to 4. Lets IPv6-only hosts reach IPv4-only servers by translating between the two.
NDA
Non-disclosure agreement. A contract that keeps shared information confidential.
NDP
Neighbor Discovery Protocol. IPv6's replacement for ARP: finds neighbors' MAC addresses and routers using ICMPv6.
NFS
Network File System. The Unix and Linux file-sharing protocol.
NFV
Network functions virtualization. Running routers, firewalls, and load balancers as virtual machines instead of dedicated hardware.
NIC
Network interface card. The adapter that connects a computer to the network, wired or wireless.
NS
Name server record. The DNS record listing the authoritative name servers for a zone.
NTP
Network Time Protocol. Synchronizes clocks across the network (UDP 123); wrong time breaks Kerberos, certificates, and logs.
NTS
Network Time Security. Authentication and integrity for NTP so time cannot be spoofed.
OFDM
Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing. The modulation that sends data across many closely spaced sub-carriers at once.
OFDMA
Orthogonal frequency-division multiple access. Wi-Fi 6 splits a channel into small sub-channels so many clients share it efficiently.
OID
Object identifier. The dotted number that names one value in an SNMP MIB.
OM1
Optical multimode 1. 62.5 micron multimode fiber, orange, the oldest grade.
OM2
Optical multimode 2. 50 micron multimode fiber, orange, 1 Gbps to about 550 m.
OM3
Optical multimode 3. Laser-optimized 50 micron multimode fiber, aqua, 10 Gbps to about 300 m.
OM4
Optical multimode 4. Higher-bandwidth 50 micron multimode fiber, aqua, 10 Gbps to about 400 m.
OS
Operating system. The software that manages hardware and runs applications: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android.
OSFP
Octal small form-factor pluggable. An eight-lane 400 Gbps module, slightly larger than QSFP-DD.
OSI
Open Systems Interconnection model. The seven-layer reference model used to describe where a protocol or device does its work.
OSPF
Open Shortest Path First. A link-state interior routing protocol that uses cost (bandwidth) as its metric and converges fast.
OT
Operational technology. Hardware and software that controls physical equipment, as opposed to IT.
OTDR
Optical time-domain reflectometer. A fiber tester that sends light pulses and measures reflections to find breaks and their distance.
OUI
Organizationally unique identifier. The first 24 bits of a MAC address, which identify the manufacturer.
PaaS
Platform as a service. The provider runs the platform (OS, runtime, database); you deploy code.
PAN
Personal area network. A network within arm's reach, such as Bluetooth between a phone and earbuds.
PAT
Port address translation. Many inside hosts share one public IP address, told apart by port numbers.
PC
Personal computer. A desktop or laptop for one user.
PCI
Payment Card Industry. The card brands' rules (PCI DSS) for anyone who stores, processes, or transmits payment card data.
PDU
Protocol data unit. The name of the chunk of data at each layer: bits, frames, packets, segments or datagrams, data.
PIN
Personal identification number. A short numeric secret, a something-you-know factor.
PKI
Public key infrastructure. The system of certificate authorities, certificates, and revocation that makes public keys trustworthy.
PoE
Power over Ethernet. Delivers DC power to devices over the data cable: 802.3af 15.4 W, 802.3at 30 W, 802.3bt 60 to 90 W.
PON
Passive optical network. Fiber to the premises using unpowered splitters between the provider and many customers.
POP3
Post Office Protocol version 3. Downloads mail to one device and usually deletes it from the server; TCP 110, secure 995.
POP3S
POP3 Secure. POP3 over TLS on TCP 995.
PSK
Pre-shared key. One shared passphrase for everyone on a Wi-Fi network (Personal mode).
PTP
Precision Time Protocol. IEEE 1588 clock sync with sub-microsecond accuracy, for finance, telecom, and industrial systems.
PTR
Pointer record. The reverse DNS record: IP address back to a name.
PVC
Polyvinyl chloride. The ordinary cable jacket, which gives off toxic smoke; plenum cable is required in air spaces.
QSFP
Quad small form-factor pluggable. A four-lane module for 40 Gbps.
QSFP-DD
Quad small form-factor pluggable double density. Eight lanes for 400 Gbps.
QSFP+
Quad small form-factor pluggable plus. Four 10 Gbps lanes: a 40 Gbps module.
QSFP28
Quad small form-factor pluggable 28. Four 25 Gbps lanes: a 100 Gbps module.
RA
Router advertisement. The IPv6 message a router sends with the prefix and gateway information hosts use for SLAAC.
RADIUS
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service. The AAA server behind Wi-Fi Enterprise, VPNs, and 802.1X; UDP 1812 and 1813.
RARP
Reverse Address Resolution Protocol. An obsolete protocol for finding an IP address from a MAC address.
RBAC
Role-based access control. Permissions are assigned to roles, and users get roles.
RC4
Rivest Cipher 4. A fast stream cipher used in WEP and old TLS; broken and deprecated.
RDP
Remote Desktop Protocol. Microsoft's remote graphical desktop on TCP 3389.
RF
Radio frequency. Radio signals; the medium of Wi-Fi, cellular, and Bluetooth, and a source of interference and, in medicine, surgical energy.
RFC
Request for Comments. The numbered documents that define internet standards, such as RFC 1918 private addresses.
RFI
Radio frequency interference. Electromagnetic interference in the radio bands, from transmitters, microwaves, and other radios.
RG-59
Radio Guide 59 coaxial cable. Thinner coax for short runs such as CCTV, often with a BNC connector.
RG-6
Radio Guide 6 coaxial cable. The modern coax grade for cable TV and cable modems, with an F-type connector.
RIP
Routing Information Protocol. The classic distance-vector protocol: hop count metric, 15-hop limit, slow.
RJ11
Registered jack 11. The small telephone plug, used for analog phone lines and DSL.
RJ45
Registered jack 45. The eight-pin plug on Ethernet twisted-pair cables (properly an 8P8C connector).
RPC
Remote procedure call. A program calls a function on another computer as if it were local.
RPO
Recovery point objective. The maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time.
RST
Reset flag. The TCP flag that aborts a connection immediately.
RSTP
Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol. The faster version of spanning tree (802.1w) that reconverges in seconds.
RTO
Recovery time objective. The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after failure.
RX
Receive. The receiving side of a link or the receiving fiber strand.
SaaS
Software as a service. Complete applications delivered over the web, such as email and office suites.
SAE
Simultaneous authentication of equals. The WPA3 Personal handshake that resists offline password guessing.
SAML
Security Assertion Markup Language. An XML standard for passing authentication between an identity provider and a web application (enterprise SSO).
SAN
Storage area network. A dedicated network that gives servers block-level access to shared disk arrays.
SASE
Secure access service edge. SD-WAN networking plus cloud-delivered security (firewall, web gateway, ZTNA, CASB) as one service.
SC
Subscriber connector. The larger square push-pull fiber connector, common on older gear and patch panels.
SCADA
Supervisory control and data acquisition. Systems that monitor and control industrial processes such as power, water, and manufacturing.
SCP
Secure Copy Protocol. Simple file copying over SSH, TCP 22.
SD-WAN
Software-defined wide area network. Steers traffic across several cheap links (broadband, LTE, MPLS) by policy from a central controller.
SDN
Software-defined networking. Separates the control plane (decisions) from the data plane (forwarding) and centralizes control.
SFP
Small form-factor pluggable transceiver. The hot-swappable module that gives a switch port its fiber or copper interface, 1 Gbps.
SFP+
Enhanced small form-factor pluggable. The 10 Gbps version of the SFP module.
SFTP
SSH File Transfer Protocol. File transfer inside an SSH session, TCP 22.
SHA-256
Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit. The standard hash today: a 256-bit fingerprint of any input.
SIEM
Security information and event management. Collects logs from everything, correlates them, and raises alerts.
SIP
Session Initiation Protocol. Sets up and tears down voice and video calls; port 5060, or 5061 with TLS.
SLA
Service level agreement. The contract stating measurable service commitments, such as 99.9% uptime.
SLAAC
Stateless address autoconfiguration. IPv6 hosts build their own address from the router's advertised prefix, no DHCP server needed.
SMB
Server Message Block. Windows file and printer sharing on TCP 445.
SMF
Single-mode fiber. A tiny core (about 9 microns) and a laser, for long distances.
SMTP
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. Sends email between servers on TCP 25; clients submit on 587 with TLS.
SMTPS
SMTP Secure. SMTP with TLS, port 465 (implicit) or 587 with STARTTLS.
SNMP
Simple Network Management Protocol. Polls and receives alerts from network devices (UDP 161 polls, 162 traps).
SNTP
Simple Network Time Protocol. A lighter version of NTP for clients that need less accuracy.
SOA
Start of authority record. The record at the top of a DNS zone: primary server, contact, serial number, and timers.
SOX
Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The US law requiring accurate financial reporting and controls, with IT audit implications.
SPAN
Switched port analyzer. A switch feature that mirrors traffic from ports or VLANs to a monitoring port.
SPF
Sender Policy Framework. A DNS TXT record listing which servers may send mail for a domain.
SQL
Structured Query Language. The language used to query databases; also the name of the servers on TCP 1433 (Microsoft) and 3306 (MySQL).
SR
Short reach. The multimode 10 Gbps optic, about 300 m on OM3.
SRV
Service record. A DNS record that locates a service: host, port, priority, and weight.
SSE
Security service edge. The security half of SASE: secure web gateway, CASB, zero trust access, delivered from the cloud.
SSH
Secure Shell. Encrypted remote command-line access and file transfer on TCP 22; replaces Telnet and FTP.
SSID
Service set identifier. The Wi-Fi network name that access points broadcast and clients join.
SSO
Single sign-on. Log in once and reach many systems without signing in again.
ST
Straight tip connector. The round bayonet twist-lock fiber connector; legacy.
STP
Spanning Tree Protocol. Blocks redundant switch links so frames cannot loop, while keeping them ready as backups. Also: Shielded twisted pair. Twisted-pair cable with foil or braid around the pairs for noisy environments; the shield must be grounded.
SVI
Switch virtual interface. A virtual Layer 3 interface on a switch that gives a VLAN an IP address and routes for it.
SYN
Synchronize flag. The first packet of a TCP handshake.
Syslog
System logging protocol. Sends device log messages to a central server on UDP 514 with severity levels 0 to 7.
T568A
TIA/EIA 568A wiring standard. One of the two pin-outs for RJ45 cables; green pair on pins 1 and 2.
T568B
TIA/EIA 568B wiring standard. The more common RJ45 pin-out; orange pair on pins 1 and 2.
TACACS+
Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus. Cisco's AAA protocol for device administration on TCP 49; encrypts the whole payload and separates authentication from authorization.
TCP
Transmission Control Protocol. Reliable, ordered, connection-based transport: three-way handshake, acknowledgments, retransmission.
TERA
TERA connector. A shielded, non-RJ45 connector used with Cat 7 cabling.
TFTP
Trivial File Transfer Protocol. Bare-bones UDP 69 file transfer with no login, used for firmware and config files.
TKIP
Temporal Key Integrity Protocol. WPA's per-packet keying scheme; deprecated.
TLS
Transport Layer Security. The encryption layer under HTTPS and most secure protocols; use 1.2 or 1.3.
TOTP
Time-based one-time password. A six-digit code from an authenticator app that changes every 30 seconds.
TTL
Time to live. A counter that keeps packets and DNS records from living forever.
TV
Television. A display or broadcast receiver; smart TVs are IoT devices.
TX
Transmit. The sending side of a link or the sending fiber strand.
TXT
Text record. A free-text DNS record, used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and domain ownership checks.
UDP
User Datagram Protocol. Connectionless, fast transport with no delivery guarantee; used for voice, video, DNS, DHCP.
UPC
Ultra physical contact. The flat, blue fiber connector polish used in most LANs.
UPS
Uninterruptible power supply. A battery unit that keeps equipment running through a power cut and conditions the power.
URL
Uniform resource locator. A web address such as https://www.example.com/page.
US
United States. The country; US standards, 60 Hz mains, and US connector conventions.
USB
Universal Serial Bus. The standard port for peripherals, storage, and charging.
UTP
Unshielded twisted pair. The standard copper network cable: four twisted pairs, no shield.
VA
Volt-ampere. The unit of apparent power used to size a UPS.
VCSEL
Vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser. The cheap laser used in multimode fiber transceivers.
VFL
Visual fault locator. A visible red laser that lights up a fiber so you can see breaks and trace strands.
VLAN
Virtual local area network. A logical LAN on a switch: ports in different VLANs are separate broadcast domains.
VLSM
Variable-length subnet masking. Using different subnet sizes inside one network so addresses are not wasted.
VM
Virtual machine. A complete computer running as software on a hypervisor.
VNI
VXLAN network identifier. The 24-bit segment ID in a VXLAN header.
VoIP
Voice over IP. Telephone calls carried as packets on the data network.
VPC
Virtual private cloud. Your isolated virtual network inside a cloud provider.
VPN
Virtual private network. An encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet.
VRRP
Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol. The open-standard first-hop redundancy protocol.
VTP
VLAN Trunking Protocol. Cisco's protocol for distributing VLAN definitions to other switches.
VXLAN
Virtual extensible LAN. Tunnels Layer 2 segments over a Layer 3 network with a 24-bit ID, giving 16 million segments instead of 4094 VLANs.
WAN
Wide area network. Connects LANs across cities or countries, usually over links leased from a provider.
WEP
Wired Equivalent Privacy. The original Wi-Fi encryption, broken in minutes; never use it.
Wi-Fi
Wireless fidelity. The trade name for IEEE 802.11 wireless networking.
WLAN
Wireless local area network. A LAN delivered over Wi-Fi instead of cables.
WLC
Wireless LAN controller. A central device that configures and manages many lightweight access points.
WPA
Wi-Fi Protected Access. The interim fix for WEP that used TKIP; deprecated.
WPA2
Wi-Fi Protected Access 2. Wi-Fi security using AES with CCMP; still common and acceptable.
WPA3
Wi-Fi Protected Access 3. The current Wi-Fi security standard: SAE in Personal mode, stronger encryption, protected management frames.
ZTNA
Zero trust network access. Every request is authenticated and authorized, regardless of where it comes from.

IPv4 addressing and subnetting 7

10.0.0.0/8 (10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255)
Private, RFC 1918
172.16.0.0/12 (172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255)
Private, RFC 1918. 172.32.x.x is public
192.168.0.0/16 (192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255)
Private, RFC 1918
169.254.0.0/16
APIPA, link-local. Means DHCP failed
255.255.255.255
Limited broadcast (DHCP Discover)
0.0.0.0/0
Default route, route of last resort
100.64.0.0/10
Carrier-grade NAT shared space

Switching 10

Standard
STP 802.1D; RSTP 802.1w; MSTP 802.1s
Root bridge
Lowest bridge ID (priority then MAC). Set core priority low
Port roles
Root port (toward root), designated port (one per link), blocked (redundant). RSTP adds alternate and backup
STP states
Blocking, listening, learning, forwarding: 30 to 50 seconds
RSTP states
Discarding, learning, forwarding: converges in seconds
PortFast
Skips listening and learning on host ports. Never on switch-to-switch links
BPDU guard
Shuts a PortFast port that receives a BPDU (rogue switch)
Root guard
Stops a downstream switch from becoming root
Loop guard
Protects against unidirectional link failures
Loop symptoms
Broadcast storm, CPU at 100 percent, MAC addresses flapping, everything slow after adding a redundant cable

DHCP, DNS, and time 9

A
Name to IPv4 address
AAAA
Name to IPv6 address
CNAME
Alias: one name to another name
MX
Mail exchanger for the domain, with priority
NS
Authoritative name servers for a zone
SOA
Start of authority: zone serial and timers
PTR
IP address back to a name (reverse zone, in-addr.arpa)
TXT
Free text: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain verification
SRV
Locates a service by name, port, and priority (SIP, Active Directory)

Network operations 18

SNMP
Agent on the device, MIB database, OID per variable. Manager polls with Get on UDP 161; device sends traps on UDP 162
SNMP versions
v1 and v2c: plaintext community string (v2c adds bulk). v3: authentication, integrity, encryption
Flow data
NetFlow, sFlow, IPFIX: who talked to whom, ports, volume. No payload. Finds top talkers
Packet capture
Protocol analyzer (Wireshark) fed by a SPAN port or an inline tap. Every byte
Syslog severity
0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug
SIEM
Correlates logs from many sources, alerts on patterns, retains for compliance
Baseline
Normal utilization, latency, errors over time. Anomaly alerts fire on deviation
Solutions
Discovery (ad hoc or scheduled), traffic analysis, performance, availability (uptime versus SLA), configuration monitoring
RPO
Recovery point objective: how much data you can lose, measured backward in time
RTO
Recovery time objective: how fast service must be restored
MTTR
Mean time to repair: average fix time
MTBF
Mean time between failures: average life before failing
Cold site
Space, power, cooling only. Days or weeks. Cheapest
Warm site
Equipment and connectivity in place; restore data. Hours to a day
Hot site
Running mirror with current data. Minutes. Most expensive
Active-active
All nodes serve; capacity drops on failure
Active-passive
Standby takes over on failure (FHRPs)
Tabletop
Walk through the plan on paper. Validation test: actually fail over or restore

EMI; use STP or fiber

Access port in the wrong VLAN
Untagged traffic lands in the wrong VLAN on a trunk
Native VLAN mismatch
Local devices reachable, nothing remote

Some hosts on the same subnet unreachable
Incorrect subnet mask
Intermittent connectivity, address conflict warning
Duplicate IP (static inside a scope without exclusion)
New clients get 169.254.x.x, old ones work
DHCP scope exhaustion or unreachable server
Ping by IP works, by name fails
DNS
One application or port fails, others work
ACL blocking it
Traffic goes out, replies never come back
Missing return route or asymmetric routing through a stateful firewall
Full signal bars, poor throughput
Interference or co-channel overlap; use 1, 6, 11 or move to 5 GHz
Choppy voice, delay varies
Jitter
Everything slow through one link at 100 percent
Bottleneck or congestion
Clients cling to a distant AP
Too little cell overlap or transmit power too high
ping
Reachability, round-trip time, loss. Loopback, self, gateway, remote in that order
traceroute / tracert
Every hop and its latency; where the path breaks. mtr and pathping repeat over time
ipconfig /all, /release, /renew, /flushdns
Windows address, mask, gateway, DNS, lease, MAC; refresh lease; clear resolver cache
ifconfig, ip addr
Linux and macOS addressing
arp -a
IP-to-MAC cache; duplicates and poisoning
nslookup, dig
Query DNS directly, pick a server, ask for a record type
netstat
Open connections and listening ports; netstat -r shows the routing table
nmap
Open ports and services; live hosts on a subnet (authorized use only)
tcpdump, Wireshark
Command-line capture; graphical protocol analyzer
LLDP / CDP
What device and port is on the other end of a cable

The device's ARP cache

Status, speed, duplex, errors, CRCs, drops

Current configuration

Toner and probe

Continuity, pinout, opens, shorts, split pairs, length

Proves a run meets its category with a report
Punch-down tool, crimper

Loopback plug
Tests a port's own transmit and receive
Visual fault locator

OTDR

Optical power meter
Received light level
Fiber cleaning kit

Wi-Fi analyzer
APs, channels, signal, dead spots
